title: Multi-Source BFS: Rotting Oranges
oneLiner: Start a BFS from EVERY rotten orange at once; each BFS layer is one minute, and the answer is how many layers it takes to reach every fresh orange.
keyTakeaway: When something spreads from several starting points at the same speed, put ALL the starting points in the queue before the first step. BFS then processes the grid in rings of equal distance, so the number of layers is the time it takes, and any fresh cell never reached means the answer is -1.
explanation:
Each cell of the grid is 0 (empty), 1 (a fresh orange) or 2 (a rotten orange). Every minute, each rotten orange rots the fresh oranges directly above, below, left and right of it. Return the number of minutes until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if some fresh orange can never be reached.

The rot spreads outward from every rotten orange at the same time and the same speed. That is exactly what breadth-first search does: it visits everything at distance 1, then everything at distance 2, and so on. The insight is to start the BFS from all the rotten oranges at once, by putting every one of them in the queue before the loop starts (a "multi-source" BFS). Running a separate BFS from each rotten orange and taking minimums would also work, but it costs O((rows × cols)²) instead of O(rows × cols).

Process the queue one layer at a time: read the queue's current size, pop exactly that many cells, and for each one rot its fresh neighbours (set them to 2 right away, so nobody rots them twice) and push them. If that layer rotted at least one orange, a minute has passed. Keep a count of fresh oranges from the initial scan and decrement it each time one rots; when the queue empties, return the minutes if the count reached 0, otherwise -1.

Two edge cases trip people up. If there are no fresh oranges at the start, the answer is 0 even if there are no rotten ones either. And if there are fresh oranges but no rotten ones, the answer is -1. The fresh-counter handles both without special cases.

The same shape solves "distance from every cell to the nearest gate" (Walls and Gates), "distance to the nearest 0" (01 Matrix) and "how long until the fire reaches you". Interviewers often ask why DFS fails here: DFS would reach a cell along a long path first and record the wrong time.

visualizationSteps.message: 0 = empty (dimmed), 1 = fresh, 2 = rotten. Scan once: both rotten oranges go into the queue together (dashed), and there are 12 fresh oranges to rot.
Minute 1: every orange in the queue rots its fresh neighbours at the same time. 3 oranges rotted (bright) and become the next layer of the queue. 9 fresh left.
Minute 2: every orange in the queue rots its fresh neighbours at the same time. 4 oranges rotted (bright) and become the next layer of the queue. 5 fresh left.
Minute 3: every orange in the queue rots its fresh neighbours at the same time. 3 oranges rotted (bright) and become the next layer of the queue. 2 fresh left.
Minute 4: every orange in the queue rots its fresh neighbours at the same time. 1 orange rotted (bright) and become the next layer of the queue. 1 fresh left.
Minute 5: every orange in the queue rots its fresh neighbours at the same time. 1 orange rotted (bright) and become the next layer of the queue. 0 fresh left.
The last layer rotted nothing new, so the queue empties. No fresh oranges remain, so the answer is 5 minutes. Starting from both rotten oranges at once is what makes each layer exactly one minute.

recognitionSignals: Something spreads or ripples out from SEVERAL starting cells at the same rate (rot, fire, infection, signal), and you need the time until it covers everything.
"Distance from each cell to the nearest X" where there are many X cells -- seed the queue with all of them.
The answer is a number of steps or minutes on an unweighted grid, which means BFS layers, not DFS.
gotchas: Mark an orange rotten (or visited) when you PUSH it, not when you pop it. Otherwise two rotten neighbours both push it and it is counted twice.
Only count a minute when the layer actually rotted something. Incrementing once per loop iteration overcounts by 1 at the end.
A grid with no fresh oranges returns 0, not -1, even if there are no rotten oranges either.
confusableWith: Grid Flood Fill: Number of Islands (this track) also spreads across a grid, but it only cares which cells are reachable, so DFS is fine. Here the number of layers matters, which needs BFS.
Graphs: BFS Traversal (Fundamentals) is the single-source version. Multi-source BFS is the same loop with more than one cell in the queue before it starts.

complexity.note: Each cell is enqueued at most once, when it rots, and each pop checks 4 neighbours. The queue can hold a large fraction of the grid at once.
